title: Linear models, design matrices and diagnostic limits
outcome: Connect an R model formula to its numerical design matrix, fitted coefficients and diagnostic assumptions.
mechanism:
An R formula specifies a model representation, not a causal identification strategy. lm turns that formula and data into a model frame and a numerical design matrix, then fits coefficients. Inspecting model.matrix makes intercepts, factor coding and interactions visible rather than treating formula notation as a black box.

A fitted coefficient describes a conditional relationship under that representation. With an interaction, a slope can depend on another predictor or group. Reporting one main-effect coefficient as a universal effect discards that structure. Factor reference levels also determine which contrasts individual coefficients represent, even when fitted predictions remain equivalent under a recoding.

Residuals compare observed outcomes with fitted means. In ordinary least squares with an intercept, the fitted residuals are orthogonal to the design columns and sum to zero up to numerical error. Those algebraic properties do not prove independent errors, constant variance, normality or a correct scientific model. Diagnostic plots and substantive knowledge investigate additional assumptions.

A rank-deficient design cannot identify every coefficient uniquely. Including a column that is exactly twice another creates redundant information. A numerical fit may retain fitted values while marking an aliased coefficient unavailable. Increasing sample count by duplicating the same redundant pattern does not create the missing distinction.

Mean confidence intervals and future-observation prediction intervals answer different questions. Under the model assumptions, a prediction interval includes residual variation in a new observation as well as uncertainty in the fitted mean, making it wider at the same point. Neither justifies extrapolation into unsupported predictor regions automatically.

vocabulary.definition: The numerical columns implied by the formula and factor coding.
Observed response minus fitted conditional mean.
A coefficient direction not separately identifiable because design columns are dependent.
An interval for a new response under the model, including residual variation.

anatomy: Fit with lm(y ~ x, data=d), inspect coef, model.matrix, fitted and residuals, and reconstruct predictions as X %*% coef(fit). Check qr(X)$rank before interpreting all coefficients. predict(..., interval="confidence") targets the fitted mean; interval="prediction" targets a future observation. A formula x*group expands to main effects and their interaction.

worked_examples.title: Reconstruct a simple fit
worked_examples.code:
d <- data.frame(x = 0:4, y = c(1, 3, 4, 7, 8))
fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = d)
X <- model.matrix(fit)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(coef(fit)), c(1, 1.8), tolerance = 1e-10)))
stopifnot(max(abs(as.numeric(X %*% coef(fit)) - fitted(fit))) < 1e-10)
stopifnot(abs(sum(residuals(fit))) < 1e-10)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(sum(residuals(fit)^2), 0.8, tolerance = 1e-10)))
print(coef(fit))
worked_examples.explanation: The coefficient and residual-sum oracles come from the small literal data. Orthogonality verifies the fitted least-squares calculation, not all distributional assumptions.
worked_examples.expected: Intercept 1, slope 1.8, residual sum near0, RSS 0.8.

worked_examples.title: Two interval targets
worked_examples.code:
d <- data.frame(x = 0:4, y = c(1, 3, 4, 7, 8))
fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = d)
new <- data.frame(x = 2)
confidence <- predict(fit, new, interval = "confidence")
prediction <- predict(fit, new, interval = "prediction")
stopifnot(confidence[1, "fit"] == prediction[1, "fit"])
stopifnot(diff(prediction[1, c("lwr", "upr")]) > diff(confidence[1, c("lwr", "upr")]))
print(confidence)
print(prediction)
worked_examples.explanation: The point estimate is shared, while the prediction interval includes additional outcome variation. The comparison relies on the same fitted model and new predictor value.
worked_examples.expected: Same fitted mean; wider future-observation interval.

exercises.prompt: Recover the design matrix for y~x on the five-row fixture.
exercises.answer: The first column is all ones and the second is x; multiplying by coefficients reconstructs fitted values.

exercises.prompt: Predict at x=5 and label its support relative to training.
exercises.hint: The training x values end at 4.
exercises.answer: The fitted value is 10; this is extrapolation beyond the observed predictor range.
exercises.expected: Prediction 10 with an explicit extrapolation qualification.

exercises.prompt: Fit y~x*group to two exact group lines A:1+2x and B:4+x.
exercises.hint: Expand the interaction columns and use A as reference.
exercises.answer: Coefficients are intercept 1, x = 2, group B coefficient 3 and interaction-1 under the declared reference coding.

exercises.hint: Compare QR rank with design column count.
exercises.answer: The design is rank deficient and at least one coefficient is aliased; fitted values do not identify both slopes uniquely.
exercises.expected: Rank below column count and an NA coefficient.

exercises.prompt: Check residual orthogonality for the simple fit.
exercises.hint: Multiply X-transpose by the residual vector.
exercises.answer: The result is approximately zero for the fitted least-squares projection. It is not a proof of independent errors.

exercises.prompt: Explain why the prediction interval is wider than the mean confidence interval.
exercises.answer: A new response includes residual outcome variation; uncertainty in its mean alone omits that variation.
exercises.expected: Correct target distinction and matched-point comparison.

reference:
d <- data.frame(x = 0:4, y = c(1, 3, 4, 7, 8))
fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = d)
X <- model.matrix(fit)
stopifnot(identical(dim(X), c(5L, 2L)), all(X[, 1] == 1))
stopifnot(max(abs(as.numeric(X %*% coef(fit)) - fitted(fit))) < 1e-10)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(predict(fit, data.frame(x = 5))), 10, tolerance = 1e-10)))
g <- data.frame(x = rep(0:2, 2), group = factor(rep(c("A", "B"), each = 3), levels = c("A", "B")))
g$y <- ifelse(g$group == "A", 1 + 2 * g$x, 4 + g$x)
interaction <- lm(y ~ x * group, data = g)
stopifnot(max(abs(unname(coef(interaction)) - c(1, 2, 3, -1))) < 1e-10)
d$double_x <- 2 * d$x
aliased <- lm(y ~ x + double_x, data = d)
stopifnot(qr(model.matrix(aliased))$rank < ncol(model.matrix(aliased)), anyNA(coef(aliased)))
stopifnot(max(abs(crossprod(X, residuals(fit)))) < 1e-10)
ci <- predict(fit, data.frame(x = 2), interval = "confidence")
pi <- predict(fit, data.frame(x = 2), interval = "prediction")
stopifnot(diff(pi[1, c("lwr", "upr")]) > diff(ci[1, c("lwr", "upr")]))
cat("r-043 reference checks passed\n")
solution_explanation:
The design-matrix reconstruction connects formula notation to the actual numerical fit. The interaction example fixes the factor reference level so the coefficient names have a defined interpretation; the two group-specific slopes remain the substantive quantities.

The alias example intentionally separates identifiable fitted values from nonunique parameter coordinates. Residual orthogonality is an algebraic least-squares property, while uncertainty intervals rely on further assumptions. The reference reports extrapolation and interval targets explicitly rather than treating predict as a scientific interpretation engine.
